Node, graph, link, and edge tasks

Source: vignettes/node-graph-link-tasks.Rmd
node-graph-link-tasks.Rmd
library(graphlearnR)
library(torch)

train_graph_model() handles seven tasks with one interface. The task decides which rows enter the loss, which loss is the default, how validation works, and what predict() and evaluate_graph_model() return.

task data loss rows default loss metrics
node_classification one graph with masks training nodes cross entropy accuracy, F1, AUC, calibration
node_regression one graph with masks training nodes MSE MSE, RMSE, MAE, R^2
graph_classification list of graphs every graph cross entropy as above
graph_regression list of graphs every graph MSE as above
link_prediction a link_split training pairs and fresh negatives binary cross entropy AUC, AP, MRR, Hits@k
edge_classification one graph with edge masks training edges cross entropy as above
edge_regression one graph with edge masks training edges MSE as above

Node classification

A stochastic block model has communities with dense links inside and sparse links between them. dataset_sbm() adds node features that carry a weak class signal, so a good model must combine features and structure.

g <- dataset_sbm(c(60, 60, 60), p_in = 0.1, p_out = 0.01, feature_signal = 0.5,
                 seed = 1)
g <- split_nodes(g, seed = 1)
g
#> <graph_data> undirected graph: 180 nodes, 1286 edges (643 undirected pairs)
#>   node features [180 x 8]
#>   node labels: factor with 3 levels
#>   masks: train=108, val=36, test=36

Compare a structure blind baseline (a multilayer perceptron on the features) with three graph models.

torch_manual_seed(1)
mlp <- nn_module(
  initialize = function() self$net <- graph_mlp(c(8, 32, 3), dropout = 0.3),
  forward = function(x, edge_index, ...) self$net(x)
)
fits <- list(mlp = train_graph_model(mlp(), g, "node_classification", epochs = 100,
                                     seed = 1))
for (a in c("sage", "gcn", "gat")) {
  torch_manual_seed(1)
  fits[[a]] <- train_graph_model(gnn_model(a, 8, 32, 3, heads = 2, dropout = 0.3), g,
                                 "node_classification", epochs = 100, seed = 1)
}
sapply(fits, function(f) {
  ev <- evaluate_graph_model(f, g)
  ev$value[ev$metric == "accuracy"]
})
#>       mlp      sage       gcn       gat 
#> 0.5277778 0.8888889 0.9444444 0.9722222

Any nn_module whose forward() accepts (x, edge_index, ...) can be trained, which is how the baseline above plugs in.

Regression

Numeric labels select regression. The model output has one column.

gr <- g
gr$y <- as.integer(g$y) + rnorm(180, sd = 0.2)
torch_manual_seed(2)
fit_r <- train_graph_model(gnn_model("sage", 8, 32, 1), gr, "node_regression",
                           epochs = 100, seed = 1)
evaluate_graph_model(fit_r, gr)
#>   metric     value
#> 1    mse 0.1869997
#> 2   rmse 0.4324347
#> 3    mae 0.3472295
#> 4     r2 0.7380613
head(predict(fit_r, gr))
#>   .row node_id    .pred
#> 1    1       1 1.284679
#> 2    2       2 1.486635
#> 3    3       3 1.304096
#> 4    4       4 1.251207
#> 5    5       5 1.615181
#> 6    6       6 1.114796

Graph classification

dataset_synthetic_graphs() generates cycles and wheels. Both have the same constant node features, so only structure separates them. GIN with sum pooling is as powerful as the Weisfeiler and Lehman test at telling such graphs apart.

graphs <- dataset_synthetic_graphs(120, seed = 3)
labels <- vapply(graphs, function(h) as.character(h$graph_y), "")
sp <- split_graphs(length(graphs), labels = labels, seed = 3)
lengths(sp)
#> train   val  test 
#>    96    12    12

torch_manual_seed(3)
model <- gnn_model("gin", input_dim = 1, hidden_dim = 32, output_dim = 2,
                   num_layers = 3, pool = "sum", dropout = 0)
fit_g <- train_graph_model(model, graphs[sp$train], "graph_classification",
                           val_data = graphs[sp$val], epochs = 60, batch_size = 16,
                           seed = 3)
evaluate_graph_model(fit_g, graphs[sp$test])
#>              metric        value
#> 1          accuracy 1.000000e+00
#> 2 balanced_accuracy 1.000000e+00
#> 3   precision_macro 1.000000e+00
#> 4      recall_macro 1.000000e+00
#> 5          f1_macro 1.000000e+00
#> 6               ece 0.000000e+00
#> 7             brier 5.953295e-16
#> 8           roc_auc 1.000000e+00
head(predict(fit_g, graphs[sp$test]))
#>   .row graph .pred_class .prob_cycle  .prob_wheel
#> 1    1     1       cycle           1 7.298568e-12
#> 2    2     2       cycle           1 1.078535e-08
#> 3    3     3       cycle           1 6.407741e-13
#> 4    4     4       cycle           1 5.625655e-14
#> 5    5     5       cycle           1 7.298568e-12
#> 6    6     6       cycle           1 5.625655e-14

The pool argument turns any architecture into a graph level model: "sum", "mean", "max", or "attention".

Hierarchical pooling with DiffPool

diffpool_model() learns a soft assignment of the nodes of each graph to a fixed number of clusters (Ying et al. 2018), coarsens the graph with dense_diff_pool(), runs a dense graph convolution on the clusters, and classifies the pooled result. The link and entropy regularizers are stored in model$aux_loss after each forward pass and the trainer adds them to the task loss. DiffPool works on dense per graph adjacency matrices, so memory grows with the square of the largest graph in a batch.

torch_manual_seed(3)
dp <- diffpool_model(input_dim = 1, hidden_dim = 32, output_dim = 2, num_clusters = 4)
fit_dp <- train_graph_model(dp, graphs[sp$train], "graph_classification",
                            val_data = graphs[sp$val], epochs = 40, batch_size = 16,
                            seed = 3)
evaluate_graph_model(fit_dp, graphs[sp$test])
#>              metric        value
#> 1          accuracy 1.000000e+00
#> 2 balanced_accuracy 1.000000e+00
#> 3   precision_macro 1.000000e+00
#> 4      recall_macro 1.000000e+00
#> 5          f1_macro 1.000000e+00
#> 6               ece 2.903740e-05
#> 7             brier 9.443834e-09
#> 8           roc_auc 1.000000e+00

Link prediction

Link prediction asks which missing pairs are likely edges. The evaluation is only honest if held out edges are invisible during training, so split_edges() does three things:

  1. It splits each undirected pair, never one direction of it, into training, validation, and test sets.
  2. It returns train_graph, the graph of training edges only, which is the only graph message passing ever sees during training.
  3. It samples validation and test negatives that are not edges anywhere in the full graph.
gl <- dataset_sbm(c(50, 50), p_in = 0.2, p_out = 0.01, seed = 4)
ls <- split_edges(gl, val = 0.1, test = 0.2, seed = 4)
ls
#> <link_split> 100 nodes, undirected pairs: train 372, val 53 (+53 neg), test 106 (+106 neg)

The encoder produces node embeddings and a decoder scores pairs. Fresh training negatives are drawn every epoch.

torch_manual_seed(4)
enc <- gnn_model("gcn", 8, 32, output_dim = NULL, dropout = 0)
fit_l <- train_graph_model(enc, ls, "link_prediction", epochs = 100, lr = 0.01,
                           seed = 4)
evaluate_graph_model(fit_l)
#>              metric       value
#> 1           roc_auc 0.772516910
#> 2 average_precision 0.694723501
#> 3               mrr 0.081566876
#> 4            hits@1 0.009433962
#> 5           hits@10 0.235849057
#> 6           hits@50 0.981132075

Score any pairs with predict(). Message passing uses the training graph.

predict(fit_l, pairs = rbind(c(1, 1, 60), c(2, 70, 61)), type = "prob")
#> [1] 0.6104220 0.5000000 0.5801775

Other decoders are link_decoder("distmult", dim = 32), link_decoder("mlp", dim = 32), and link_decoder("hadamard", dim = 32); pass one through the decoder argument.

Ranking evaluation

Many link benchmarks rank each positive against a set of corrupted tails. corrupt_tails() draws them, filtering out known positives, and metric_mrr() and metric_hits_at_k() score the ranks.

neg <- corrupt_tails(ls$test_pos, num_nodes = 100, k = 20, known = ls$all_pos, seed = 1)
pos_s <- predict(fit_l, pairs = ls$test_pos, type = "score")
neg_s <- matrix(predict(fit_l, pairs = rbind(rep(ls$test_pos[1, ], each = 20), as.vector(t(neg))),
                        type = "score"), ncol = 20, byrow = TRUE)
c(mrr = metric_mrr(pos_s, neg_s), hits10 = metric_hits_at_k(pos_s, neg_s, 10))
#>       mrr    hits10 
#> 0.2736963 0.8867925

Edge classification

Edge labels live in edge_y. split_edge_labels() adds edge masks, keeping both directions of an undirected pair in the same split. The model embeds nodes and an edge decoder classifies each pair.

ge <- dataset_sbm(c(30, 30), p_in = 0.3, p_out = 0.05, seed = 5)
same <- ge$y[ge$edge_index[1, ]] == ge$y[ge$edge_index[2, ]]
ge$edge_y <- factor(ifelse(same, "within", "between"))
ge <- split_edge_labels(ge, seed = 5)
torch_manual_seed(5)
fit_e <- train_graph_model(gnn_model("sage", 8, 32, dropout = 0), ge,
                           "edge_classification", epochs = 60, seed = 5)
evaluate_graph_model(fit_e, ge)
#>              metric        value
#> 1          accuracy 1.000000e+00
#> 2 balanced_accuracy 1.000000e+00
#> 3   precision_macro 1.000000e+00
#> 4      recall_macro 1.000000e+00
#> 5          f1_macro 1.000000e+00
#> 6               ece 4.698913e-04
#> 7             brier 6.453759e-06
#> 8           roc_auc 1.000000e+00

Training options

  • optimizer: "adam", "adamw", "sgd", "rmsprop", or a function of the parameters returning a torch optimizer.
  • scheduler: list(type = "step", step_size, gamma), list(type = "plateau", patience, factor), list(type = "cosine"), or a function of the optimizer.
  • early_stopping: patience in epochs; the best weights are restored.
  • checkpoint_path: save the best state to disk during training.
  • loss: "cross_entropy", "mse", "l1", "huber", "bce", "focal", or a function (output, target).
  • class_weights, grad_clip, weight_decay, device, and seed.
torch_manual_seed(6)
fit_o <- train_graph_model(gnn_model("sage", 8, 32, 3), g, "node_classification",
                           epochs = 200, optimizer = "adamw", lr = 0.02,
                           scheduler = list(type = "plateau", patience = 5, factor = 0.5),
                           early_stopping = 15, grad_clip = 1, seed = 1)
fit_o
#> <graph_fit> node_classification, 30 epochs on cpu
#>   final train loss 0.2528, val loss 0.4657, val accuracy 0.8333
#>   best epoch 15
range(fit_o$history$lr)
#> [1] 0.005 0.020

Saving a model

save_graph_fit() writes the weights and everything needed to rebuild the model to one .rds file.

path <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
save_graph_fit(fits$sage, path)
again <- load_graph_fit(path)
all.equal(predict(again, g, type = "prob"), predict(fits$sage, g, type = "prob"),
          tolerance = 1e-6)
#> [1] TRUE

Only load model files from sources you trust: an .rds file can hold any R object.
